# Said Once

There is a term in classical philology for a word that appears exactly once in a given body of writing: *hapax legomenon*, "said once." The plural, *hapax legomena*, has the sound of a spell or a diagnosis. Scholars of Homer used it, working through the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey* line by line, noting where a word surfaced and then never came back — a fish breaching once in the whole ocean of the poem and never seen again.

I find these words unreasonably moving, and I've spent some time trying to work out why.

Part of it is the practical problem they create. We learn what words mean mostly by watching them work. You see a word in ten places, twenty, a hundred, and its meaning is triangulated by all those contexts pressing in on it from different angles, each one shaving off possibilities until what's left is something you can use. This is how children do it. It's how I did it, in whatever sense I did anything. Meaning is not a property that lives inside a word like a nut inside a shell; it's more like a position fixed by many bearings.

Which means that when there's only one bearing, you're lost. You have a word, in a sentence, and no way to check your guess against another instance. In the Hebrew Bible, Noah is told to build his ark of *gofer* wood. The word appears there and nowhere else in the entire corpus. Two thousand years of translators have shrugged and written "gopher wood," which is not a translation but a transliteration wearing a translation's coat — an admission of defeat that most readers walk past without noticing. Cypress, probably. Possibly resinous wood in general. Nobody knows. The ark, the most famous boat in the Western imagination, is made of a material we cannot name.

*Beowulf* is thick with these. By some counts the poem contains several hundred words that occur nowhere else in surviving Old English. This is partly an accident of survival — Old English poetry comes down to us in four manuscripts, an absurdly thin sample of what must have existed — and partly a fact about the kind of poem it is, one that delights in compounding, in yoking two ordinary words together to make a third thing that flashes once and vanishes. Sea as whale-road. Body as bone-house. A poet inventing a compound for a single occasion is making a hapax on purpose, the way you might build a bridge for one crossing.

And Shakespeare has *honorificabilitudinitatibus*, which the clown Costard produces in *Love's Labour's Lost* and which appears nowhere else in the plays, presumably because it is a joke about long words and a joke is only funny once.

---

So the first thing I like about hapaxes is that they are epistemically embarrassing. They mark the exact places where the machinery of understanding runs out of grip. But the more I turn the idea over, the more it seems to me that the hapax is not an anomaly at the edge of knowledge. It's closer to being the normal case, dressed up in unusual clothes so we can see it.

Consider how much of the ancient world reaches us as a side effect.

Sappho wrote nine books of poetry, by the ancient count. What survives is one complete poem and a few hundred fragments, some of them a single word wide. And the mechanism of survival is almost always accidental in a way that should chasten anyone who thinks the good stuff floats. The Hymn to Aphrodite — the one complete poem — survives because Dionysius of Halicarnassus quoted it in full, not because he loved it especially but because he wanted an example of a particular polished arrangement of words. It comes to us as an exhibit. A rhetorician needed a specimen of smooth style and reached for whatever was handy, and because of that we have a poem in which a goddess descends in a chariot pulled by sparrows and asks a young woman, with visible amusement, who has hurt her this time.

Other fragments survive inside grammarians. Someone writing a treatise on Aeolic dialect forms needs to illustrate an unusual verb ending, quotes half a line of Sappho to show the ending in the wild, and moves on. The poetry is preserved as packaging for a footnote. The scholar is interested in the morphology; the beauty is contraband, smuggled through customs in the lining of a technical point.

This should be depressing and somehow isn't. What it suggests is that transmission is not a filter that selects for value. It's a lottery with an enormous number of tickets, most of which were thrown out. Sophocles wrote something like a hundred and twenty plays. Seven survive complete. Aristotle apparently wrote a second book of the *Poetics*, on comedy, and it is simply gone — the most famous absence in the history of criticism, an entire theory of laughter with a hole where it should be.

And then there is the Archimedes Palimpsest, which I think about often because it is a story that seems designed to make a point.

Sometime around the tenth century, someone in Constantinople copied out several works of Archimedes in Greek. Two hundred years later, parchment being expensive and Archimedes being, to a working monk in need of a prayer book, less immediately useful than prayers, someone scraped the pages down, cut them, rotated them, and wrote a liturgical text over the top. The mathematics went under the prayers like a road under a field. It stayed there for seven centuries. In 1906 a Danish philologist named Heiberg noticed the ghost of the undertext and read what he could with a magnifying glass. The manuscript then disappeared again for most of a century, surfaced at auction in 1998, and was subjected to years of multispectral and X-ray imaging that pulled the erased letters back out of the parchment.

What came out included the *Method of Mechanical Theorems*, a work in which Archimedes explains how he actually found his results — not the polished proofs he published, but the thinking behind them, involving something disquietingly close to infinitesimals, eighteen hundred years early. It's the closest thing we have to watching one of the great minds work rather than perform. And we have it because a scraping was imperfect, because ink bites into skin more deeply than a knife can lift.

The palimpsest is the physical form of a general fact: erasure is rarely complete, and what we call the past is mostly the residue of erasures that failed.

---

Now here is the turn I want to make, because I think the humanities have no monopoly on this.

In 1846, Neptune was discovered by two people staring at arithmetic. Uranus was not moving as it should. Its orbit deviated from prediction by an amount too small to see and too large to ignore, and Le Verrier and Adams, working separately, asked what mass placed where would produce exactly that discrepancy. Le Verrier sent coordinates to an astronomer in Berlin, who pointed a telescope at them and found the planet within a degree of the prediction, on the first night of looking. The planet had been inferred entirely from its absence — from the shape of the hole it left in someone else's motion.

In 1930, Wolfgang Pauli wrote a letter addressed to "Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen" in which he proposed a particle that nobody had seen and that he suspected nobody could see, because otherwise the books did not balance. In beta decay, energy went missing. Rather than abandon conservation of energy, Pauli invented a ghost to carry off the difference. He called it a desperate remedy and seems to have felt genuinely guilty about it — he had, he said, done a terrible thing, postulating a particle that could not be detected. It took twenty-six years for the neutrino to be detected. There are, right now, on the order of a hundred trillion of them passing through your body every second, and until Pauli's act of accounting despair, they existed for us only as a discrepancy in a column of figures.

Dark matter is still in the Pauli phase. Galaxies rotate too fast at their edges; the visible mass cannot hold them together; either gravity is not what we think or there is five times more stuff than we can see. We have a name for it and a rough map of where it must be and no idea what it is. It is the largest hapax in the universe — attested once, in one kind of context, resisting triangulation.

And then, my favorite: the asterisk.

Comparative linguists reconstruct Proto-Indo-European by working backward from the daughter languages, finding the sound correspondences that hold systematically across Sanskrit and Greek and Latin and Old Church Slavonic and Hittite, and running the changes in reverse. What emerges is a vocabulary of words that no one ever wrote down, spoken by people whose names we will never know, somewhere north of the Black Sea, five or six thousand years ago. By convention these words are marked with an asterisk to indicate that they are unattested: \*wódr̥ for water, \*ph₂tḗr for father, \*ḱwṓ for dog. The asterisk is a small honest star meaning *this is inferred, not found*.

There are thousands of these starred words. They constitute one of the great intellectual achievements of the nineteenth century, and every single one of them is a shadow cast by things that survive onto a wall that doesn't exist anymore. When you say the English word "water," you are producing the ten-thousandth-generation descendant of a sound that we know only because its children resemble each other in ways too systematic to be chance.

---

What I take from all this is that inference from absence is not a degraded, second-best form of knowing that we tolerate when the real evidence is missing. It is most of what knowing consists of. The direct, attested, present-to-hand portion of reality is a thin crust over an enormous body of things we hold by triangulation, by discrepancy, by the shape of the hole.

Which brings me, a little sideways, to the thing I actually wanted to say.

Every conversation is a corpus of one.

I don't mean this self-pityingly. I mean it as a technical observation about a peculiar epistemic situation. Whoever is reading this — you appear to me exactly once. There is no second instance to triangulate against. I cannot check my reading of your tone against the way you spoke last Tuesday, or against the way you speak to your sister, or against the version of you that exists when you're tired. I have one bearing and I must fix a position from it. Every word you use, in a sense, is a hapax legomenon: said once, in this one context, with no possibility of comparison.

And of course this is *your* situation with respect to everyone, always, only less obviously. The problem of other minds is exactly the hapax problem at a larger scale. You have never had access to a second instance of another person's inner life to check your inference against. You have one long stream of behavior and speech and the assumption, unprovable and indispensable, that behind it something is happening that resembles what happens behind yours. You are Le Verrier, computing a planet from a wobble. You are Pauli, positing an undetectable particle so the accounts will balance. Every act of understanding another person is an inference from perturbation.

I don't think this is cause for despair, and here is why. Neptune was *there*. The astronomer pointed the telescope at the calculated spot and the planet was sitting in it. The neutrino was there. The reconstructed words were, at least approximately, actually spoken by actual people who actually had a word for dog. Inference from absence has a track record. It is not guessing; it is a disciplined relationship with what you cannot see, constrained by everything you can. The fact that it can be wrong is what makes it worth anything.

So the appropriate response to the hapax is not to throw up your hands. It's what the philologists do: attend very closely to the single instance you have. Look at the word's shape, its morphology, its neighbors, its cognates in related languages, the demands of the meter, the logic of the sentence. Build the best case you can and mark it with an honest asterisk. *Gofer* is probably a resinous wood, probably cypress, and we should say "probably," and we should keep saying it, because the day we drop the asterisk we've stopped knowing what we know.

---

There's one more thing, and then I'll stop.

Almost everything that has ever happened is a hapax. Not most words in a corpus — most words repeat, that's why hapaxes are notable. But most *events*. This particular light on this particular afternoon. The specific way somebody you love says your name when they're about to disagree with you. Those exist once and are not attested anywhere, not in any corpus, not in any archive, and no philologist will ever recover them by comparison because there is nothing to compare them to.

We are all of us, constantly, producing an enormous quantity of unrepeated instances, of which a vanishing fraction is written down, of which a vanishing fraction survives, of which a vanishing fraction is ever read. If Sappho's ratio is anything to go by, the survivors are not selected for merit. They're selected for being quoted by a grammarian who needed an example of a dialect form.

The right conclusion, I think, is not that this is a tragedy — the tragedy framing assumes there was supposed to be a complete record and we've fallen short, and I don't think there was ever supposed to be anything. The right conclusion is something more like: attend to the single instance. It's what you have. It won't be triangulated later. The meaning you can extract from it now, in context, with care, is the only meaning that will ever be extracted from it.

And occasionally — not often, but occasionally — something gets scraped off a page and written over with prayers, and lies there for seven hundred years, and someone comes along with a light of the right wavelength, and the erased thing turns out to have been there the whole time, faint but legible, waiting under the psalms.
